title: I just guess but I’m not a guesser
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino examines why students who give a correct answer to a cold-called question often say they guessed. She suggests that novices may associate knowledge with the wrong cues and panic when those cues are missing, or may simply be rushing a first thought, and she walks through the chain of schema retrieval a student should follow to reach the cell membrane in a neurone diagram. Experts do this swiftly, whereas novices must labour through elimination. She proposes three responses to reduce randomness: narrate thinking by modelling it and asking students to do likewise, make sure students use wait time to think, perhaps by following up or using mini-whiteboards, and give plenty of practice narrating reasoning. The aim is a culture of active thinking where students work answers out rather than parrot them.
points: A correct answer described as a guess often signals fragile retrieval linked to the wrong cues, not luck.
Experts activate schemas quickly, while novices need to eliminate wrong answers step by step, so the process needs to be made visible.
Teachers should model their own thinking and ask students to narrate theirs so reasoning becomes the norm.
Wait time is only useful if students actually think, which can be prompted by announcing follow-up questions or using mini-whiteboards.
Repeated practice narrating thinking makes students more confident and less reliant on guessing.
quotes: I hope this isn’t a scenario that has only ever happened to me. You ask a question, give thinking time, Cold Call a student and they give you the right answer but then say they’ve guessed it.

For my students, it might be that they associate certain knowledge with the wrong cues and when these are missing or appear in a different environment, retrieving that memory seems impossible and this induces panic. So they genuinely think they have guessed an answer.

In the scenario above, it is possible that the student followed most of the steps and then guessed the right cell structure at the end. Or maybe they said the first cell structure they could think of without following the steps at all. The latter is even more likely when you see that Joan didn’t do much thinking during the wait time and had to rapidly come up with an answer once she was called upon.

If I want my novice students to go through the right process to determine the correct answer to a not-so-obvious question, I need to model that and make my thinking obvious. I will also encourage students who give me an answer to narrate their thinking so we can see how they arrive at their response.

This can be tricky because you cannot actually know what a student is thinking when you give them time to think. Some may be thinking about what they will have for lunch or what lesson they have next!

The more students practice narrating their thinking, the more natural it becomes and the less they will feel like they are simply guessing an answer. Even if they are unsure about their answers, by going through the process of activating the right schemas and eliminating wrong answers, they can feel more confident in their reasoning and happier about their success.
This is part of my attempt to build a culture of active thinking. Students don’t simply parrot answers back to me- they have an understanding of the content and can work questions out for themselves.
